lessons.title: POI: definition, diagnosis and work-up of the cause
lessons.objective: Apply the diagnostic criteria of the 2024 ESHRE/ASRM/CRE-WHiRL/IMS guideline (disordered cycles for at least 4 months and one FSH > 25 IU/l), place AMH as a supporting rather than primary test, recognise where NICE NG23 differs, and order the recommended causal work-up: karyotype, FMR1 premutation, 21-hydroxylase antibodies and TSH.
lessons.closing: Under 40, at least 4 months of disordered cycles and one FSH > 25 IU/l are enough for ESHRE; a second FSH only if there is doubt. Then: karyotype and FMR1 in all non-iatrogenic POI, 21-hydroxylase antibodies if the cause is unknown, and TSH. And the diagnosis is conveyed with time and sensitivity.

lessons.title: POI: consequences, hormone therapy and follow-up
lessons.objective: Explain the consequences of untreated POI (life expectancy, heart, bone, muscle, cognition, sexuality and mental health), prescribe hormone therapy until the usual age of menopause at adequate doses, compare HRT and the combined contraceptive according to ESHRE and NICE, organise follow-up and place complementary therapies honestly.
lessons.closing: In POI, hormone therapy is not only for symptoms: it is recommended until the usual age of menopause to protect heart, bone and brain, and adherence matters as much as the choice of preparation. Complementary approaches can accompany it, never replace it.

lessons.title: POI and fertility: natural conception, oocyte donation and preservation
lessons.objective: Give an honest estimate of the chance of natural conception, explain that no intervention has been shown to increase it, present oocyte donation with its obstetric risks and the nuances of sister donation, and recognise when fertility preservation is possible.
lessons.closing: POI is not always final: ovarian activity and spontaneous pregnancy can occur, but they are unlikely. Nothing reliably increases the chance; oocyte donation is the established option, and preservation only makes sense before the risk materialises.

items.title: POI: loss of ovarian activity before age 40
items.core: The 2024 guideline defines premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) as loss of ovarian activity before age 40, characterised by amenorrhoea or irregular cycles with elevated gonadotropins and low estradiol. Between 40 and 44 it speaks of early menopause, which is outside the guideline's scope. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]
items.body:
The reported prevalence of non-iatrogenic POI ranges from about 1% in older studies to 3.5% in recent publications, and may vary with characteristics such as ethnicity. The age-40 cut-off lies approximately two standard deviations below the usual age of menopause (50 ± 4 years). [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]

The group recommends using the term “premature ovarian insufficiency” in practice and research. The guideline does not apply to low ovarian reserve: the two can be confused, but they are distinct entities with different management needs. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]
items.recall: How does the 2024 guideline define POI, and what does it call loss of ovarian function between 40 and 44?
items.pearl: With a prevalence of up to 3.5%, POI is not a rare disease: think of it in any woman under 40 with irregular cycles or symptoms of estrogen deficiency.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE/ASRM/CRE-WHiRL/IMS 2024: rec. 1 GPP; recs 2 and 3 guideline group “statements” (ungraded). GPP = good practice point based on the group's clinical expertise (ungraded).

items.title: 2024 diagnosis: 4 months of disordered cycles and one FSH > 25 IU/l
items.core: ESHRE recommends diagnosing POI with spontaneous amenorrhoea or irregular cycles for at least 4 months and an elevated FSH > 25 IU/l. FSH is repeated after 4–6 weeks only if there is diagnostic uncertainty, and it does not need to be timed to a specific cycle day. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]
items.body:
This is a change from 2015/2016, when two FSH measurements were required; now a single one, together with the characteristic clinical picture, is considered sufficient, which speeds up diagnosis and the start of treatment. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]

Before diagnosing: exclude pregnancy; remember that hormonal contraception (oral, injectable or long-acting) can conceal or cause amenorrhoea and lower FSH, and that some, such as the combined oral contraceptive, may need to be stopped to confirm the diagnosis. Bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy before 40 is already POI and needs no further testing. Diagnosis is not based on estradiol, although a low estradiol with a raised FSH supports it. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]
items.recall: What duration of disordered cycles, what FSH threshold and how many measurements does ESHRE 2024 require to diagnose POI?
items.pearl: FSH does not require day 3: if the patient has had months of amenorrhoea, order it now.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE/ASRM/CRE-WHiRL/IMS 2024: rec. 8 strong, ⊕⊕○○; recs 9, 10 and 11 GPP. On the guideline's GRADE scale, ⊕⊕⊕⊕ = high, ⊕⊕⊕○ = moderate, ⊕⊕○○ = low and ⊕○○○ = very low; strength (strong/conditional) and quality are different things. GPP = good practice point (ungraded). ⊕ symbols come from the summary article (Hum Reprod Open 2024); recommendation numbers from the full guideline.

items.title: ESHRE 2024 versus NICE NG23: one or two FSH tests, and where AMH fits
items.core: NICE NG23 (2015 POI recommendations, unchanged in the 2026 version) requires raised FSH on 2 samples 4–6 weeks apart and advises against diagnosing on a single blood test; the 2024 ESHRE guideline accepts one FSH > 25 IU/l and keeps a second for uncertainty. [[ref:nice-2026-ng23]] [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]
items.body:
On AMH they agree on the essentials: NICE says not to use it routinely to diagnose POI. ESHRE recommends against using it as the primary diagnostic test (strong), accepts that it may help confirm the diagnosis when FSH is inconclusive, interpreted in its clinical context, and advises against routine testing to predict POI because of insufficient evidence of accuracy. [[ref:nice-2026-ng23]] [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]

NICE gives no numerical FSH threshold and, if the diagnosis is in doubt, recommends referral to a specialist in menopause or reproductive medicine. [[ref:nice-2026-ng23]]
items.recall: Where do NICE NG23 and ESHRE 2024 disagree on the number of FSH tests, and what role do both give AMH?
items.pearl: Much of the disagreement reflects timing: NICE has not revised its POI section since 2015, and ESHRE moved from two FSH tests to one in 2024.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: NICE NG23 1.7.2, 1.7.3, 1.7.4, 1.7.5 [2015]. ESHRE/ASRM/CRE-WHiRL/IMS 2024: rec. 12 strong, ⊕○○○; recs 9, 13 and 14 GPP. On the guideline's GRADE scale, ⊕⊕⊕○ = moderate, ⊕⊕○○ = low and ⊕○○○ = very low; strength and quality are different things.

items.title: Genetic causes: karyotype and FMR1 premutation in all non-iatrogenic POI
items.core: ESHRE recommends karyotyping and FMR1 (fragile X) premutation testing for all women with non-iatrogenic POI, without restricting access by age. After comprehensive genetic counselling, and where available, additional testing such as next-generation sequencing (NGS) can be offered. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]
items.body:
Chromosomal abnormalities affect about 10–13% of women with POI, mostly of the X chromosome (aneuploidies, mosaicism and structural defects). The FMR1 premutation (55–200 CGG repeats) is the most common single-gene disorder linked to POI: it is found in 1–5% of sporadic POI and up to 13% with a family history. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]

FMR1 premutation must be ordered as a specific test, because multigene panels and NGS do not detect it. Its genetic counselling should cover the associated disorders (such as fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome, FXTAS) and the possibility of expansion to a full mutation in offspring, which causes fragile X syndrome. Discuss the implications before any genetic test, and offer counselling and testing to relatives if the premutation or another genetic cause is identified. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]
items.recall: Which two genetic tests does ESHRE recommend in all non-iatrogenic POI, and why is an NGS panel not enough for fragile X?
items.pearl: A “normal” NGS panel does not rule out the FMR1 premutation: order it separately.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE/ASRM/CRE-WHiRL/IMS 2024: recs 18 and 19 strong, ⊕⊕○○; rec. 20 conditional, ⊕⊕○○; recs 17, 21 and 32 GPP. Prevalence figures from the full guideline text (pp. 51–52 and 58). On the guideline's GRADE scale, ⊕⊕○○ = low quality; strength and quality are different things.

items.title: Autoimmunity: 21-hydroxylase antibodies and TSH yes; anti-ovarian and routine TPO antibodies no
items.core: In POI of unknown cause, ESHRE recommends screening for 21-hydroxylase antibodies; in addition, in every woman with POI, TSH should be measured at diagnosis and repeated every 5 years or when symptoms arise. Anti-ovarian antibodies should not be used to diagnose autoimmune POI, and TPO antibodies should not be ordered routinely. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]
items.body:
If 21-hydroxylase antibodies are positive, refer to endocrinology to assess adrenal function; if negative, they need not be repeated later unless signs or symptoms of adrenal insufficiency develop. An abnormal TSH requires evaluation and treatment of the thyroid disorder. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]

The group advises against routine TPO antibody screening because of their high prevalence in the general population. Tell the patient about the different causes, the limits of current knowledge and testing, and that a specific cause may not be found. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]
items.recall: Which antibody is screened in POI of unknown cause, what happens if it is positive, and how often is TSH repeated?

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE/ASRM/CRE-WHiRL/IMS 2024: recs 22, 23, 24, 26, 27 and 28 strong, ⊕○○○; recs 15 and 25 GPP. On the guideline's GRADE scale, ⊕○○○ = very low quality: strong recommendations on very low evidence; strength and quality are different things.

items.title: Conveying the diagnosis and thinking about the family
items.core: The group recommends conveying a POI diagnosis compassionately and sensitively, giving personalised evidence-based information, leaving time for questions, sharing decisions, supporting continuity of care and referring to support groups and mental health care. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]
items.body: Female relatives (sisters, daughters) of a woman with non-iatrogenic POI should be told they are at increased risk of developing it. The group recommends offering them support, telling them the signs and symptoms so they seek advice promptly, and explaining that there are no established methods to predict or prevent POI; ovarian reserve testing may be helpful, and some may wish to plan their family or consider fertility preservation. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]
items.recall: What should the sisters or daughters of a woman with non-iatrogenic POI be told according to ESHRE?
items.application: “Your ovaries are not working as expected for your age. It is not your fault, and it can be treated: the most important thing now is to look after your heart, your bones and your well-being. Take all the time you need to ask questions; we will decide things together.”

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE/ASRM/CRE-WHiRL/IMS 2024: recs 29, 30, 31, 34, 35 and 36 GPP; rec. 33 strong, ⊕⊕○○. GPP = good practice point (ungraded); recommendations informed by women with lived experience of POI. The patient phrase is an editorial suggestion, not guideline text.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman (fictional case), off hormonal contraception for a year, has had 5 months of amenorrhoea with hot flushes. A pregnancy test is negative and one FSH, not timed to the cycle, is 58 IU/l. According to the 2024 ESHRE/ASRM/CRE-WHiRL/IMS guideline, what is most appropriate?

options.text: Diagnose POI with this FSH and start the causal work-up.
options.why: Correct: at least 4 months of disordered cycles and one FSH > 25 IU/l are enough; a second FSH is only needed if there is doubt.

options.text: Always repeat FSH after 4–6 weeks before diagnosing.
options.why: That was the 2015/2016 criterion and remains NICE NG23's, but ESHRE 2024 keeps repetition for diagnostic uncertainty.

options.text: Repeat FSH on cycle day 3, because an untimed result is not valid.
options.why: The guideline states that FSH for diagnosing POI does not have to be timed to a specific cycle day.

options.text: Confirm the diagnosis with a low estradiol before labelling it.
options.why: The group does not recommend diagnosing on estradiol; a low estradiol only adds confirmation.

items.explanation: The 2024 update simplified diagnosis so as not to delay treatment: a compatible clinical picture for at least 4 months and one FSH > 25 IU/l, after excluding pregnancy and the effect of hormonal contraceptives.

items.stem: According to ESHRE 2024, what is the role of AMH in POI?

options.text: It is the primary diagnostic test and replaces FSH.
options.why: ESHRE recommends (strong) against using AMH as the primary diagnostic test.

options.text: It may help confirm the diagnosis when FSH is inconclusive, interpreted in its clinical context.
options.why: Correct: it is a guideline good practice point for cases of diagnostic uncertainty.

options.text: It should be ordered routinely in young women to predict who will develop POI.
options.why: The group advises against routine testing to predict POI because of insufficient evidence of accuracy.

options.text: It has no role, and NICE recommends it instead in two measurements.
options.why: NICE NG23 says not to use AMH routinely to diagnose POI; NICE's two measurements are of FSH.

items.explanation: AMH is a supporting tool when in doubt, not for diagnosis or prediction; the guideline also notes it is not universally available.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman (fictional case) with newly diagnosed non-iatrogenic POI brings an NGS panel of POI genes with no findings. What does ESHRE indicate?

options.text: No further genetic testing is needed: the normal panel rules out genetic causes.
options.why: Multigene panels and NGS do not detect the FMR1 premutation, and karyotyping is still recommended.

options.text: Order a karyotype and a specific FMR1 premutation test, after discussing their implications.
options.why: Correct: both are strong recommendations in all non-iatrogenic POI, and FMR1 requires a specific test.

options.text: Skip genetic testing because she is over 35.
options.why: The group recommends that age should not be used to restrict access to genetic testing.

options.text: Order only anti-ovarian antibodies to confirm an autoimmune cause.
options.why: Anti-ovarian antibodies should not be used to diagnose autoimmune POI (strong).

items.explanation: The FMR1 premutation is the most common single-gene disorder linked to POI and has implications for offspring and relatives; that is why it is always ordered, and specifically.

items.stem: In a woman with POI of unknown cause, which autoimmune work-up does ESHRE recommend?

options.text: 21-hydroxylase antibodies and TSH; if the antibodies are positive, refer to endocrinology.
options.why: Correct: both are strong recommendations, and positive 21-hydroxylase antibodies require adrenal function testing.

options.text: Routine TPO antibodies, because autoimmune thyroiditis is the most frequent association.
options.why: The group advises against routine TPO antibodies because of their high prevalence in the general population.

options.text: Anti-ovarian antibodies to confirm autoimmune POI.
options.why: They should not be used to diagnose autoimmune POI (strong recommendation).

options.text: Repeat 21-hydroxylase antibodies every year even if negative.
options.why: If negative, they need not be repeated unless signs or symptoms of adrenal insufficiency develop.

items.explanation: TSH is measured at diagnosis and every 5 years or when symptoms arise; 21-hydroxylase antibodies are tested once in POI of unknown cause.

items.title: Untreated POI is associated with reduced life expectancy: heart, bone and muscle
items.core: ESHRE says to inform women that POI without hormone therapy is associated with reduced life expectancy, largely due to cardiovascular disease, and with increased risk of coronary artery disease, heart failure and stroke. It is also associated with abnormal bone microarchitecture and reduced bone mineral density. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]
items.body:
The guideline suggests informing women that POI may be associated with a higher risk of osteoporosis and fracture later in life, and with reduced muscle mass, strength and performance, with a possible risk of sarcopenia. Non-use of hormone therapy is associated with more cardiovascular events and mortality. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]

To reduce cardiovascular, bone and muscle risk, it recommends encouraging a healthy lifestyle: no smoking, a healthy diet, regular physical activity (with weight-bearing exercise for bone) and a healthy weight. Resistance exercise may be considered when muscle parameters are impaired, although POI-specific evidence is lacking; testosterone or other interventions should not be offered for muscle health because their effect is uncertain. All women with Turner syndrome should be evaluated by a cardiologist with expertise in congenital heart disease. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]
items.recall: What mainly explains the reduced life expectancy of POI without hormone therapy, and which three organs or systems does the guideline highlight?

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE/ASRM/CRE-WHiRL/IMS 2024: recs 37, 57, 77, 78 and 79 strong, ⊕⊕○○; rec. 58 conditional, ⊕○○○; rec. 71 conditional, ⊕⊕○○; rec. 73 conditional, ⊕○○○; rec. 75 strong, ⊕○○○; recs 39, 60 and 72 GPP. On the guideline's GRADE scale, ⊕⊕○○ = low and ⊕○○○ = very low: the data are mainly observational.

items.title: Cognition, sexuality and mental health: ask and treat
items.core: POI is associated with increased risk of cognitive impairment and dementia, and ESHRE recommends hormone therapy until the usual age of menopause to reduce that possible risk. The diagnosis can significantly affect psychological well-being, quality of life and sexual function. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]
items.body:
Offer psychological and quality-of-life assessment to all, with accessible psychological support, and routinely and sensitively ask permission to discuss sexuality, with a biopsychosocial approach. Hormone therapy may improve sexual function, although the effect is generally small. Transdermal testosterone at doses approximating physiological premenopausal concentrations can be considered for hypoactive sexual desire disorder (strong recommendation in iatrogenic and conditional in non-iatrogenic POI, after excluding other causes); it is safe short term, but long-term safety data are lacking. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]

For genitourinary symptoms, offer vaginal estrogen, including when they are not fully relieved by systemic therapy, and lubricants or moisturisers; laser or thermal energy is not recommended as standard care because the evidence is inconclusive. Before bilateral oophorectomy under age 45, discuss the possible effect on cognition and the risk of dementia, parkinsonism and other neurological diseases. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]
items.recall: What does ESHRE recommend for hypoactive sexual desire in POI, and what do we know about its long-term safety?

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE/ASRM/CRE-WHiRL/IMS 2024: recs 96, 97, 84, 86, 91 and 92 strong, ⊕○○○; recs 98, 87, 120 and 122 strong, ⊕⊕○○; recs 99, 90 and 121 conditional, ⊕⊕○○; recs 93 and 94 conditional, ⊕○○○; recs 85, 88, 89 and 95 GPP. On the guideline's GRADE scale, ⊕⊕○○ = low and ⊕○○○ = very low.

items.title: Hormone therapy until the usual age of menopause, with or without symptoms
items.core: ESHRE recommends hormone therapy in POI until the usual age of menopause as primary prevention of morbidity and mortality, whether or not there are estrogen-deficiency symptoms, and also to treat those symptoms. To optimise bone density it suggests a daily dose of no less than 2 mg oral estradiol or 100 µg transdermal estradiol, or equivalent. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]
items.body:
In the full guideline's regimen table, “POI” estradiol doses are 75–100 µg/24 h by patch and 2.0–4.0 mg orally, versus 25–50 µg and 1.0–2.0 mg for low or standard doses. With a uterus, always add a progestogen to prevent endometrial hyperplasia and cancer, and increase its dose when the estrogen dose is high; unscheduled bleeding needs assessment. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]

Avoid delayed initiation and non-adherence; adherence is key to minimising long-term health risks, which is why long-term follow-up is needed. Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) is not a contraceptive. With intermittent ovarian function and a wish for natural pregnancy, the HRT recommendation does not change and does not reduce that chance; a sequential regimen is recommended. On reaching the usual age of menopause, decide whether to continue on an individual risk–benefit assessment. Compounded “bio-identical” preparations are not recommended because of a lack of efficacy and safety data. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]
items.recall: Until when is hormone therapy recommended in POI, and what minimum estradiol dose does ESHRE suggest for bone?
items.pearl: In POI, hormone therapy is above all replacement: it aims to approximate what the ovary should still be producing at that age. It is not risk-free, but there is no evidence that it increases breast cancer risk compared with women of the same age without POI. Low doses designed for usual-age menopause may fall short.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE/ASRM/CRE-WHiRL/IMS 2024: rec. 38 strong, ⊕○○○; recs 101, 62, 108 and 118 strong, ⊕⊕○○; rec. 63 conditional, ⊕○○○; rec. 64 strong, ⊕○○○; recs 102, 103, 104, 109, 110 and 117 GPP. “POI” doses from table VII of the full guideline (p. 197). On the guideline's GRADE scale, ⊕⊕○○ = low and ⊕○○○ = very low.

items.title: HRT or combined contraceptive: what ESHRE and NICE say
items.core: NICE recommends offering a choice of HRT or a combined hormonal contraceptive, unless contraindicated, and continuing it until at least the age of natural menopause. ESHRE notes that the limited evidence suggests physiological HRT may be more beneficial and lower risk, and that the contraceptive is a reasonable alternative if contraception is needed or adherence improves. [[ref:nice-2026-ng23]] [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]
items.body:
If the combined oral contraceptive is used, ESHRE recommends a continuous or extended regimen to provide uninterrupted estrogen and avoid bone loss during pill-free days. Most contain ethinylestradiol, which provides more steroid than needed, with unfavourable effects on lipids and haemostasis and a higher thromboembolic risk; a small study showed lower blood pressure with a “physiological” HRT regimen. Contraceptives containing estradiol or estetrol have no comparative thromboembolic risk studies, so their indication in POI remains contraception. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]

NICE explains that HRT may have a more beneficial effect on blood pressure than a combined oral contraceptive, that both offer bone protection and that HRT is not a contraceptive. [[ref:nice-2026-ng23]]
items.recall: If a woman with POI chooses the combined oral contraceptive, which regimen should she take according to ESHRE, and why?
items.pearl: If your patient prefers the pill, do not use it in the classic regimen with a pill-free week: continuous or extended.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: NICE NG23 1.7.6 and 1.7.7 [2015]. ESHRE/ASRM/CRE-WHiRL/IMS 2024: rec. 65 strong, ⊕⊕○○; rec. 116 strong, ⊕⊕○○; rec. 115 GPP; the HRT–contraceptive comparison is guideline justification text (pp. 190 and 196), not a graded recommendation. In the guideline, “HT” is used generically and the combined oral contraceptive is treated as one of its options (rec. 65).

items.title: Follow-up: DXA, cardiovascular risk, thyroid and regular clinical review
items.core: Where available, ESHRE recommends a bone density scan (DXA) at diagnosis for all. If it is normal and adequate hormone therapy is started and adhered to, repeating it within 5 years adds little; with osteoporosis or low bone density, it is repeated every 1–3 years according to individual risk. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]
items.body:
A fall in bone density should prompt a review of hormone therapy and other factors. Calcium and vitamin D may be required if vitamin D status or calcium intake is inadequate. Other drugs, such as bisphosphonates, only with advice from an osteoporosis specialist and with particular caution if pregnancy is desired. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]

Assess cardiovascular risk at diagnosis: at least annually, blood pressure, weight and smoking status; a lipid profile and diabetes screening at diagnosis, and thereafter according to findings and global risk. Measure TSH every 5 years or when symptoms arise, consider sarcopenia screening at diagnosis, and schedule a regular clinical review focused on individual risk factors and adherence. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]
items.recall: With a normal DXA at diagnosis and good adherence to hormone therapy, does repeating it after a year make sense according to ESHRE?

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE/ASRM/CRE-WHiRL/IMS 2024: recs 67 and 66 strong, ⊕⊕○○; recs 68, 69, 59 and 24 strong, ⊕○○○; rec. 61 conditional, ⊕⊕○○; recs 70, 76, 80, 82, 83 and 119 GPP. On the guideline's GRADE scale, ⊕⊕○○ = low and ⊕○○○ = very low. The guideline acknowledges that the optimal interval for repeating DXA is uncertain.

items.title: Myth: natural approaches can replace hormone therapy in POI
items.core: ESHRE recommends that complementary therapies should not replace hormone therapy, because there is insufficient evidence that they prevent the long-term sequelae of POI. For other nutrient supplements and herbal medicines, it says to inform women that there is insufficient evidence to support their use. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]
items.body:
On Chinese herbal medicine for symptoms and metabolic risk, it says to inform women that evidence of benefit is limited but it does not appear to cause significant harm in the short term. Evidence on acupuncture for symptoms in POI is limited and does not suggest benefit from adding it to hormone therapy. The group recommends asking about the use of complementary therapies and incorporating the patient's values and preferences into shared decision-making. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]

Non-hormonal pharmacological and non-pharmacological treatments that are effective in peri- and postmenopausal women may be considered, although POI-specific evidence is lacking. A healthy lifestyle has metabolic and heart benefits in the general population, although evidence on lifestyle interventions in POI is limited; even so, the group recommends encouraging it in everyone. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]
items.recall: What does ESHRE say about using complementary therapies instead of hormone therapy in POI, and about acupuncture?
items.pearl: From an integrative gynaecology perspective, complementary approaches add value as support chosen by the patient; what they cannot do is take the place of the estrogen that protects her heart, bones and brain.

evidence.label: insufficient
evidence.note: ESHRE/ASRM/CRE-WHiRL/IMS 2024: recs 135, 136, 137 and 138 strong, ⊕○○○; rec. 133 conditional, ⊕○○○; rec. 139 strong, ⊕⊕○○; recs 134 and 140 GPP. On the guideline's GRADE scale, ⊕○○○ = very low: the guideline strongly recommends telling women about the lack of evidence.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman (fictional case) with POI has no hot flushes or other symptoms and asks whether she needs hormone treatment. According to ESHRE, what would you tell her?

options.text: Without symptoms it is not needed; it is kept for when they appear.
options.why: Hormone therapy is recommended as primary prevention whether or not there are estrogen-deficiency symptoms.

options.text: It is recommended until the usual age of menopause to reduce morbidity and mortality, even without symptoms.
options.why: Correct: a strong ESHRE recommendation, in line with NICE, which advises continuing it until at least the age of natural menopause.

options.text: Only for 5 years, because of breast cancer risk.
options.why: The guideline states there is no evidence that hormone therapy increases breast cancer risk compared with women of the same age without POI.

options.text: Calcium, vitamin D and exercise are enough.
options.why: They are useful additions in some cases, but the guideline recommends hormone therapy to protect bone, heart and cognition.

items.explanation: In POI, estrogen is replacement, not only symptomatic treatment: non-use of hormone therapy is associated with more cardiovascular events, mortality, bone loss and dementia risk.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman (fictional case) with POI does not want pregnancy and prefers the combined oral contraceptive to HRT. What is most appropriate according to ESHRE and NICE?

options.text: Refuse it: only HRT is indicated in POI.
options.why: NICE offers a choice of HRT or a combined contraceptive, and ESHRE considers it a reasonable alternative if contraception is needed.

options.text: Prescribe it in the classic 21-day regimen with a 7-day break.
options.why: Pill-free days leave periods of estrogen deficiency and bone loss; ESHRE recommends avoiding them.

options.text: Accept it in a continuous or extended regimen, explaining that the limited evidence somewhat favours HRT.
options.why: Correct: a strong recommendation for a continuous or extended regimen, within shared decision-making.

options.text: Use low-dose HRT, which is also contraceptive.
options.why: HRT is not a contraceptive, according to ESHRE and NICE, and low doses may be insufficient for bone.

items.explanation: Both guidelines accept the combined contraceptive; ESHRE asks for a continuous or extended regimen and notes that physiological HRT may be more beneficial (lower blood pressure, better lipid and thrombotic profile).

items.stem: A woman with POI (fictional case) had a normal DXA at diagnosis and has taken HRT with good adherence for a year. What does ESHRE say about the next bone density scan?

options.text: Repeat it every year while POI lasts.
options.why: The 1–3-year interval is for osteoporosis or low density, not for a normal DXA with good adherence.

options.text: Repeating it within 5 years is of low value.
options.why: Correct: a strong recommendation (⊕○○○), although the guideline acknowledges that the optimal interval for repeating DXA is uncertain.

options.text: The initial DXA was unnecessary: FRAX is enough.
options.why: Where available, DXA at diagnosis is recommended for all women with POI.

options.text: Add a preventive bisphosphonate and repeat after 6 months.
options.why: Other drugs such as bisphosphonates are only considered with advice from an osteoporosis specialist, with caution if pregnancy is desired.

items.explanation: Bone follow-up is risk-adapted: DXA at diagnosis, and repeat every 1–3 years only with low density or osteoporosis; a fall prompts review of hormone therapy.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman (fictional case) with POI wants to stop HRT and replace it with acupuncture and a phytoestrogen supplement. According to ESHRE, what is most appropriate?

options.text: Accept the switch, because acupuncture has solid evidence in POI.
options.why: Evidence for acupuncture in POI is limited and does not suggest benefit from adding it to hormone therapy.

options.text: Forbid any complementary therapy.
options.why: The group recommends asking about them and incorporating the patient's values and preferences into shared decision-making.

options.text: Explore her reasons and explain that these therapies should not replace HRT because there is no evidence they prevent long-term sequelae.
options.why: Correct: a strong recommendation not to replace hormone therapy, within shared decision-making that respects her preferences.

options.text: Switch to compounded “bio-identical” preparations as a middle ground.
options.why: They are not recommended because of a lack of efficacy and safety data.

items.explanation: Complementary therapies can coexist with hormone therapy if the patient wishes, but the lack of evidence on preventing bone, cardiovascular and cognitive sequelae means they cannot replace it.

items.title: Spontaneous pregnancy: possible but unlikely, and nothing increases it
items.core: POI substantially reduces natural conception, but in non-surgical POI ovarian activity may resume: the guideline estimates natural conception of up to 15% in those women, probably < 5% overall. So, if pregnancy is not wanted, contraception is recommended. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]
items.body:
In a cohort of 358 women with idiopathic POI, 25% later showed ovarian activity, mostly within the first year, and 4.8% became pregnant; in another of 507, 23% resumed activity, with a 15.3% pregnancy rate among them versus 3.5% for the whole cohort. If natural pregnancy occurs, the cause of POI should be considered in case it has implications for the pregnancy or child, such as the FMR1 premutation. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]

ESHRE says to inform women that no intervention has been reliably shown to increase ovarian activity or natural conception. In vitro activation, mesenchymal stem cells and intraovarian platelet-rich plasma have been studied without adequate controls or sufficient power, and none can currently be recommended. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]
items.recall: What chance of natural conception does ESHRE estimate in non-surgical POI, and what is the practical consequence if pregnancy is not wanted?
items.pearl: “Unlikely” is not “impossible”: if she does not want pregnancy, she needs contraception, and HRT is not contraception.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE/ASRM/CRE-WHiRL/IMS 2024: recs 40, 41 and 42 strong, ⊕○○○; rec. 43 strong, ⊕⊕⊕○. Cohort figures and estimate from the justification (full guideline, pp. 84–86). On the guideline's GRADE scale, ⊕⊕⊕○ = moderate and ⊕○○○ = very low.

items.title: Oocyte donation and fertility preservation: what to offer and when
items.core: ESHRE says to inform women that oocyte donation is an established option to achieve pregnancy after a POI diagnosis, and NICE NG257 considers it effective in POI, including after treatment. Fertility preservation can be considered before a treatment that may cause POI, but in most women already diagnosed it is not possible because the follicle pool is depleted. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.body:
If the donor is a sister, in non-iatrogenic POI women must be told about the shared genetic risk and the higher rate of stimulation cycle cancellation: in one small analysis (13 sister and 66 altruistic donations), 30.7% with sisters versus 6.1% with altruistic donors, with similar oocyte numbers and pregnancy rates in completed cycles. If there is a known genetic cause, such as the FMR1 premutation, the sister should be tested before stimulation. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]

Oocyte donation pregnancies are high risk and should be managed in an appropriate obstetric unit, encouraging disclosure of their origin to the team. Before pregnancy, investigate the cause of POI and assess cardiometabolic and thyroid function; in Turner syndrome, comprehensive cardiac screening and counselling by maternal–fetal medicine and cardiology. Natural pregnancies after idiopathic POI or most chemotherapy show no higher obstetric or neonatal risk than the general population. Identify women with risk factors for POI to counsel them about the risk and fertility preservation. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]
items.recall: What must be explained to a woman with non-iatrogenic POI who plans to receive oocytes from her sister?

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE/ASRM/CRE-WHiRL/IMS 2024: recs 44, 45, 48, 49, 52 and 54 strong, ⊕⊕○○; rec. 55 strong, ⊕○○○; rec. 46 conditional, ⊕⊕○○; recs 5 and 47 GPP; cancellation figures from the justification (full guideline, p. 86). NICE NG257 1.52.1 [2004, amended 2026]. On the guideline's GRADE scale, ⊕⊕○○ = low and ⊕○○○ = very low.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman (fictional case) with idiopathic POI, on HRT, does not want pregnancy for now and asks whether she needs contraception. According to ESHRE, what would you tell her?

options.text: No: with POI, spontaneous pregnancy is impossible.
options.why: In non-surgical POI ovarian activity may resume, and there is a chance of natural conception.

options.text: No: HRT already works as her contraceptive.
options.why: HRT is not a contraceptive; both ESHRE and NICE ask for this to be explained.

options.text: Yes: although unlikely, she can conceive, so contraception is recommended if she wants to avoid pregnancy.
options.why: Correct: a strong ESHRE recommendation in non-surgical POI.

options.text: Yes, but only if AMH is detectable.
options.why: The contraception recommendation applies to all non-surgical POI when pregnancy is to be avoided, without making it conditional on any test, including AMH.

items.explanation: The guideline estimates natural conception of up to 15% in women who resume ovarian activity and probably < 5% overall: little, but not zero.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman (fictional case) with non-iatrogenic POI wants a pregnancy. She has been offered intraovarian platelet-rich plasma, and her sister offers to donate oocytes. According to ESHRE, what is most appropriate?

options.text: Do the platelet-rich plasma first, because it has been shown to reactivate the ovary.
options.why: No intervention has been reliably shown to increase ovarian activity; PRP has been studied without adequate controls and cannot be recommended.

options.text: Offer oocyte donation and explain that, with her sister, there is a shared genetic risk and more cycle cancellations.
options.why: Correct: donation is the established option, and counselling about sister donation is a strong recommendation.

options.text: Cryopreserve her own oocytes before deciding.
options.why: In most women with POI there is no opportunity for preservation because the follicle pool is depleted.

options.text: Use the sister's oocytes without further work-up, because they share favourable genetics.
options.why: Shared genetics is precisely a risk; if there is a known genetic cause, the sister should be tested before stimulation.

items.explanation: Oocyte donation is the most successful treatment in POI; the resulting pregnancy is high risk and should be managed in an appropriate obstetric unit.

items.title: Case: Irene, Hugo and amenorrhoea at 32

steps.text: Irene (fictional case), 32, stopped her contraceptive a year ago to try for a pregnancy with Hugo. After months of irregular cycles she has had 5 months of amenorrhoea, with hot flushes. Pregnancy test negative and FSH 58 IU/l. Under ESHRE 2024, one FSH > 25 IU/l with at least 4 months of disordered cycles is enough; NICE NG23 would ask for a second sample after 4–6 weeks. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng23]]

She is given the diagnosis with time for questions. After explaining their implications, a karyotype and a specific FMR1 premutation test, 21-hydroxylase antibodies and TSH are ordered. The karyotype is 46,XX, FMR1 shows no premutation, the antibodies are negative and TSH is normal. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]

A baseline DXA is done, blood pressure, weight, lipids and glucose are measured, and she is offered psychological assessment and contact with a support group. It is explained that hormone therapy is recommended until the usual age of menopause to reduce morbidity and mortality, with or without symptoms, not just for the hot flushes. Irene fears hormone treatment will “take away” her chance of pregnancy: ESHRE states that, if there is evidence of intermittent ovarian function and a wish for natural pregnancy, HRT does not reduce that chance and a sequential regimen is recommended. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]

Irene asks about a supplement “to reactivate the ovary”. She is told there is insufficient evidence for supplements or herbal medicines, that they should not replace hormone therapy and that no intervention has been shown to increase natural conception; her chance of spontaneous pregnancy exists but is low. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]]

A year later, without a pregnancy, Irene and Hugo consider oocyte donation, and her sister offers to donate. They are told it is the established option, about the shared genetic risk and higher cancellations with a sister donor, and that the pregnancy will be high risk and should be managed in an appropriate obstetric unit, with prior cardiometabolic and thyroid assessment. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]

eshre-2024-poi.title: Evidence-based guideline: premature ovarian insufficiency
eshre-2024-poi.authors: POI Guideline Group (ESHRE, ASRM, CRE-WHiRL, IMS); Panay N, Anderson RA, Bennie A, Cedars M, Davies M, Ee C, Gravholt CH, Kalantaridou S, Kallen A, Kim KQ, Misrahi M, Mousa A, Nappi RE, Rocca WA, Ruan X, Teede H, Vermeulen N, Vogt E, Vincent AJ
eshre-2024-poi.population: Women with premature ovarian insufficiency (loss of ovarian activity before age 40), spontaneous or iatrogenic, and their relatives. 2024 update of the 2015/2016 ESHRE guideline, developed with ASRM, CRE-WHiRL and IMS; co-published in Human Reproduction Open, Fertility and Sterility and Climacteric. It does not apply to low ovarian reserve.
eshre-2024-poi.finding: 145 recommendations. Diagnosis with disordered cycles for at least 4 months and a single FSH > 25 IU/l (repeat after 4–6 weeks only if there is uncertainty); AMH is not the primary diagnostic test. Karyotype and FMR1 premutation in all non-iatrogenic POI; 21-hydroxylase antibodies if the cause is unknown; TSH at diagnosis and every 5 years. Hormone therapy until the usual age of menopause, with or without symptoms; if the combined oral contraceptive is used, in a continuous or extended regimen. No intervention reliably increases natural conception; oocyte donation is the established option. Complementary therapies should not replace hormone therapy.
eshre-2024-poi.limitations: Recommendations and ⊕ symbols read in the Europe PMC open-access XML version of the summary article (PMC11631070); recommendation numbers, justifications and tables read in the full guideline (ESHRE PDF, 254 pp., where the ⊕ symbols do not extract). For most management options, POI-specific evidence is limited: almost 76% of the evidence-based recommendations are strong even where the evidence was limited to low or very low quality observational data; many recommendations are extrapolated from women at the usual age of menopause.

nice-2026-ng23.title: Menopause: identification and management (NG23)
nice-2026-ng23.authors: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
nice-2026-ng23.population: People in perimenopause and menopause in the UK health system; section 1.7 covers premature ovarian insufficiency in people under 40. Published November 2015, last updated 15 April 2026.
nice-2026-ng23.finding: POI (1.7, 2015 recommendations): diagnosis with symptoms, including infrequent or absent periods, and raised FSH on 2 samples 4–6 weeks apart; do not diagnose on a single blood test or use AMH routinely. Offer replacement with HRT or a combined hormonal contraceptive, until at least the age of natural menopause unless contraindicated; HRT may have a more beneficial effect on blood pressure than a combined oral contraceptive; both offer bone protection; HRT is not a contraceptive.
nice-2026-ng23.limitations: Full PDF (105 pp., 15-04-2026 version) read. The POI recommendations have not been updated since 2015 and predate the 2024 ESHRE guideline (which requires a single FSH). It gives no numerical FSH threshold. UK health-system context.

nice-2026-ng257.title: Fertility problems: assessment and treatment (NG257)
nice-2026-ng257.authors: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
nice-2026-ng257.population: People with fertility problems in the UK health system.
nice-2026-ng257.finding: Do not use AMH to predict clinical pregnancy through spontaneous conception (1.18.3). Use AMH or AFC as predictors of ovarian response to inform decisions and counselling about the likelihood of live birth after assisted conception (1.18.4). Do not use FSH as a predictor (1.18.5). Refer at presentation if the woman is 36 or over or there is a known cause or predisposing factors (1.16.8); otherwise investigation after 1 year of unprotected intercourse.
nice-2026-ng257.limitations: NHS (UK) context; replaces CG156. Numbering checked in the March 2026 PDF.
